messages.content:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: HighErrorRate on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}
Alert raised: 2026-10-24T15:06:02Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires: that wait is part of the time from the onset to the alert - count it before calling detection slow. The alert came 2 minutes 2 seconds {after_the_wait} after that wait ended. Its condition looks back over 1 minute {rule_looks_back}: up to that much of the time from the onset to the alert is that window filling - count it before calling detection slow.
Broken from 2026-10-24T14:59:00Z {began} (the onset) to 2026-10-24T15:07:00Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 8 minutes {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 1 minute 40 seconds {held}, until 2026-10-24T15:08:04Z {argus_stopped}. That is how long the response took, not how long the fault lasted - leave it out of your answer.
Error rate before it began: 1.0% {errors_before}.
Error rate while it was broken: 29.1% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 35.5% {errors_at_worst}.
Rise above baseline: 28.0% {errors_rise} of traffic failed that otherwise would not have.
The series behind the alert, `sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[1m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[1m]))` - its alert said "Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 1.0166666666666666% {series_before} before it began, 29.0625% {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 35.5% {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
Customer loss: 5,182.30 USD {customer_loss} - how far the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier, beyond how much those hours vary on their own.

What Argus did, in order:
  - [T1] 2026-10-24T15:06:23Z {T1.1} Argus: Received HighErrorRate on io-shop
  - [T2] 2026-10-24T15:06:27Z {T2.1} Argus: Moved the incident to INVESTIGATING - a worker took the incident up
  - [T3] 2026-10-24T15:06:28Z {T3.1} Argus: Called in the Investigator Agent
  - [T4] 2026-10-24T15:06:36Z {T4.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's per-minute metrics, anchored on 15:06:02 {T4.2}
  - [T5] 2026-10-24T15:06:40Z {T5.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 360 {T5.2} minutes of metrics
  - [T6] 2026-10-24T15:06:41Z {T6.1} Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 14:59 {T6.2}
  - [T7] 2026-10-24T15:06:41Z {T7.1} Investigator Agent: Recorded where the 3 {T7.2} replicas run - all on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB
  - [T8] 2026-10-24T15:06:42Z {T8.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 {T8.2} day before Oct 24 14:59 {T8.3}
  - [T9] 2026-10-24T15:06:43Z {T9.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 1 {T9.2} production change
  - [T10] 2026-10-24T15:06:44Z {T10.1} Investigator Agent: Read how far the deployment had rolled out - all 3 {T10.2} replicas run one revision, which the history does not name
  - [T11] 2026-10-24T15:06:44Z {T11.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's log lines, the 37 {T11.2} minutes 2 {T11.3} seconds before 15:06:02 {T11.4}
  - [T12] 2026-10-24T15:06:44Z {T12.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 135 {T12.2} log lines
  - [T13] 2026-10-24T15:06:46Z {T13.1} Investigator Agent: Formed 1 {T13.2} candidate cause, best first: C1
  - [T14] 2026-10-24T15:06:46Z {T14.1} Investigator Agent: Read every channel available
  - [T15] 2026-10-24T15:06:46Z {T15.1} Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 1 {T15.2} flag change by anyone but Argus, the 1 {T15.3} hour before 15:06:46 {T15.4}
  - [T16] 2026-10-24T15:06:50Z {T16.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATING to act on the leading candidate
  - [T17] 2026-10-24T15:06:50Z {T17.1} Argus: Called in the Mitigation Agent
  - [T18] 2026-10-24T15:06:50Z {T18.1} Mitigation Agent: Reverted the feature flag monthly-spend-feature, moved from ON to OFF
  - [T19] 2026-10-24T15:07:19Z {T19.1} Mitigation Agent: Waiting to see whether the service is still at the incident's level, from 15:07 {T19.2} - up to 120s {T19.3}
  - [T20] 2026-10-24T15:08:03Z {T20.1} Mitigation Agent: Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 15:07 {T20.2}
  - [T21] 2026-10-24T15:08:03Z {T21.1} Mitigation Agent: Judged the action CONFIRMED
  - [T22] 2026-10-24T15:08:04Z {T22.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATED - set flag [monthly-spend-feature] OFF and the rule that fired stopped firing
  - [T23] 2026-10-24T15:09:23Z {T23.1} Code-Fix Agent: Proposed a fix as a draft pull request - https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/336

Changes to production it read:
  - [P1] 2026-10-24T14:59:00Z {P1.1} flag-toggle monthly-spend-feature by admin: feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on
  - Deploys read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:
  - [G7e5d] INFO io-shop: monthly-spend-feature=off - 200 {G7e5d.1} evaluations - 30 {G7e5d.2} occurrences in 30 {G7e5d.3} minutes, 14:29–14:58 {G7e5d.4}
  - [Gad41] INFO io-shop: account pages rendered normally - 4 {Gad41.1} occurrences in 30 {Gad41.2} minutes, 14:29–14:58 {Gad41.3}
  - [G46bc] ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ClientDisconnected: the shopper closed the connection - 44 {G46bc.1} occurrences in 31 {G46bc.2} minutes, 14:30–15:00 {G46bc.3}
  - [Gbac1] WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - 34 {Gbac1.1} occurrences in 37 {Gbac1.2} minutes, 14:30–15:06 {Gbac1.3}; # was 0.50 {Gbac1.4} to 35.50 {Gbac1.5}, typically 1.50 {Gbac1.6}, highest at 15:05 {Gbac1.7}
  - [G971b] 14:59 {G971b.1} INFO io-shop: monthly-spend-feature=off 146 {G971b.2} / on 54 {G971b.3} - 200 {G971b.4} evaluations
  - [G5309] ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ZeroDivisionError: division by zero at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47 - 15 {G5309.1} occurrences in 8 {G5309.2} minutes, 14:59–15:06 {G5309.3}
  - [Gce95] INFO io-shop: monthly-spend-feature=on - 200 {Gce95.1} evaluations - 7 {Gce95.2} occurrences in 7 {Gce95.3} minutes, 15:00–15:06 {Gce95.4}

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - cite them; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1] The monthly-spend-feature flag was switched on at the onset. This enabled a code path that raises ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47, so account page requests failed and the error rate rose from about 1% {C1.1} to about 32% {C1.2}. No deployment or config change is involved, and the rollout had converged. [feature-flag-toggle, confidence 0.93 {C1.3}, confirmed]

Actions it took:
  - [M1] Reverted the feature flag monthly-spend-feature (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault is in `average_spend_per_item_this_month` in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. It divides `account.total_this_month_cents` by the number of purchases flagged `in_current_month`. For a shopper who has bought before but not this month, that number is 0 {F1.1}, so it raises ZeroDivisionError at line 47 {F1.2}. That is a common shopper, and the existing test helper calls it "the ordinary case". Turning on monthly-spend-feature sends those shoppers down this path, which is why account page errors rose to about 32% {F1.3}.
      
      The fix: if nothing was bought this month, return 0 {F1.4}. That is the real answer for "average spend per item this month" when nothing was spent this month. It is not a hidden failure. It keeps the `int` return type that `render_spend_summary`, `account_page._the_figure_for` and `RenderedPage.figure_cents` depend on, and nothing is caught or swallowed. With the flag off, nothing changes. The lifetime path (`average_spend_per_item`) is untouched, so the existing test that expects ZeroDivisionError for an account with no purchase history ever still holds. Callers in account_page.py need no change.
      
      The new tests in tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py cover the case directly and through `render_spend_summary` with `use_monthly_summary=True`. Against the current code both raise ZeroDivisionError. With this change they should return 0 {F1.5}. Nothing has run them yet.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, done): Reverted the feature flag monthly-spend-feature
  - AI-2 (prevent, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
PR #336 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.
The document already states what set it off, in a section of its own: the change [P1].

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

action_items.item: Roll out io-shop feature flag changes, such as monthly-spend-feature, in stages that halt automatically when the account page error rate rises.
In CI, run the account page tests with each feature flag switched on, and require them to pass before that flag can be switched on in production.
Route the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop so that it pages the on-call person.
Keep monthly-spend-feature off until a fix for shoppers with no purchases this month is deployed.

causal_chain.step: Account page requests failed. The share of requests answered with a server error went from {errors_before} before the onset to {errors_while_broken} while the service was broken, and peaked at {errors_at_worst}.
From the onset, account page requests raised ZeroDivisionError in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. No such error was logged before the onset, when account pages rendered normally.

ruled_out.what: A deploy. No deploy came back for the day before the onset, and the flag switch was the only production change read.

The revision the replicas were running. All replicas ran one revision as of {T10.1}, and no deploy was read in the day before. The service was back to normal with that revision still in place once only the flag had been switched back off.
Another flag change. The flag provider's history shows one flag change by anyone but Argus in the hour read: the switch of monthly-spend-feature.

causal_chain.step: From the onset, account page requests evaluated monthly-spend-feature as on, which sent them down the monthly spend summary code. Admin switched the flag on at {P1.1}. Evaluations were all off before then, partly on at {G971b.1}, and on from then until the alert. Switching the flag back off ended the failures.

With the flag on, `average_spend_per_item_this_month` divides the account's spend this month by the number of purchases made this month. For a shopper who has bought before but not this month, that number is {F1.1}, so the division raises ZeroDivisionError at line {F1.2}.

input.cause_in_plain_words: An administrator switched on a setting that adds a new monthly spending summary to shoppers' account pages, and that summary likely breaks because it divides by the number of purchases made this month, which is none for shoppers who have bought before but not this month.

contributing_factors.factor: No test was seen that runs the monthly spend summary for a shopper who has bought before but not this month. In the files Code-Fix read, the existing test helper calls this shopper the ordinary case, and the only test seen that expects ZeroDivisionError covers the lifetime path for an account with no purchases ever.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A test like that would have failed on the division before anyone switched the flag on in production, so the fault would have been caught before it reached shoppers.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: The flag went from off to on for every evaluation within about a minute. No staged rollout and no check that stops a flag change when errors rise were seen.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A staged rollout that halts when the account page error rate rises would have kept the failures to a small slice of shoppers and switched the flag back off sooner.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

went_well: The Investigator tied the onset to the one production change it read: the switch of monthly-spend-feature.
The Mitigation Agent switched the flag back off {T18.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised, and confirmed the service was out of the incident's level {T21.1 - T18.1} after the revert.
Code-Fix proposed a fix as draft pull request PR #336 {T23.1 - T22.1} after the incident was marked mitigated.
went_wrong: The alert paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.

input.root_cause: With monthly-spend-feature on, account pages call `average_spend_per_item_this_month` in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. That function divides the account's spend this month by the number of purchases flagged `in_current_month`. For a shopper who has bought before but not this month, that number is {F1.1}, so the function raises ZeroDivisionError at line {F1.2} and the account page request fails.
input.still_at_risk: The faulty division is still in the running code, so switching monthly-spend-feature back on would likely make account pages fail again for shoppers who have bought before but not this month.
input.symptom: Account pages failed for many shoppers

content.content:
Your postmortem was not accepted:
  - your answer says [a minute] in words - write a figure the incident gave as the name shown after it, braces and all, or a working of two such names ({a - b}, {a / b}), and say any other size with no number in it ("most requests", "several minutes")

Call submit_postmortem again with the whole answer, corrected.

system.text:
You write the postmortem for an incident Argus has already handled. One message describes it - what Argus did and read, the candidate causes, the actions and what they came to, and every figure already measured - and you answer by calling submit_postmortem. Nothing is left to look up.

The candidates are the Investigator's account, written while the incident ran and before anything was tried. The record - the lines saying what Argus did, the changes, the log lines, the actions and their verdicts - is what happened. Where the two disagree, the record is right.

Write causal_chain as the five whys. The first step is the symptom: what the people using the service saw, with the evidence that shows it. The symptom field is that step in a few words, and the two must agree. Each step after it answers why the step before happened - one cause, no jumps - and cites its evidence from the record, never a candidate: a candidate is a hypothesis, and the chain says what happened. Five is a guide, not a quota: stop where the evidence stops. The root_cause field says the mechanism: the step of the chain that says why the change broke the service.

A why the record cannot answer - a missing test, a missing safeguard, an alert that came late - is a contributing factor rather than a step, and each contributing factor names an action item that answers it. Where one why has several answers, follow the one that leads to the fault and make the others contributing factors.

Never stop at a person. Where somebody's action set the incident off, ask why the system let that action do harm - why it was possible at all - and carry on from there.

tools.description: Submit the postmortem for this incident. Every field is required. Write no figure yourself anywhere in your answer - no time, duration, percentage, count or amount, not in digits and not spelled out in words. Every figure you are shown is followed by its name in braces, like {A3} or {duration}: where your prose states one, write its name, braces and all, and the document writes the figure in. A figure you were not shown but could work out from two you were - the span between two instants, how far one share is above another, how many times one is the other - is written as that working, braces and all: {back_to_normal - began}, {T3.1 - alert_raised}, {errors_at_worst / errors_before}. The document works it out from the figures as you were shown them. Say any other size with no number in it, not even in a word - "most requests", "for several minutes", never "twenty minutes", "a third" or "tripled". A number is a figure even with a unit or a clock's marks on it (5m, 10ms, 3x, 12:05Z). Any other word with a digit in it is a name - a label you cite (T2, G3fa2, C1, AI-1), a version (v2), a revision, a pod - and is written as given. State only what the evidence you are shown says: where the record does not show something - a check that was or was not run, how many replicas - leave it out or say it was not seen.

action_items.description: What should be done that the record does not already hold, each one thing a person could take on: two things to do are two items. Empty where the record's own items answer every factor. Propose nothing to confirm a cause the record already confirmed - a mitigation that worked, a hypothesis marked confirmed - and no check of what the evidence you are shown already shows: a diff states what changed. Where an F row says to check something a D row shows, say what the D row shows, and the item is what follows from it.

answers.description: The labels of the contributing factors it answers: CF-1. Empty where it answers none.

assumptions.description: Anything else the reader should know was assumed rather than measured. Empty is a valid answer.

causal_chain.description: The cause as the five whys, from the symptom down: the first step is what users saw - or, where nobody using the service saw anything wrong, that and what was seen instead - and each step after it answers why the step directly before it happened. The first why says why the symptom happened, not the symptom again in more detail. Where the incident needed two things at once - something going wrong, and nothing in place to contain it - follow the one that leads to what set it off; the other is one of the contributing_factors, not named in the chain. A safeguard that did not stop it is never a step of its own: it is one of the contributing_factors. Every step cites at least one piece of evidence by its label. Date a change by its own row's instant - the T or P row that records it - never by an effect it had. A state a row read - how many replicas run a revision, which way a flag is set - is known as of the row that read it, by that row's instant, which is its first figure, as T3.1 is T3's - not from when the change was made. What else the record ruled out - an earlier change, a flag the provider showed unchanged, a candidate refuted - goes in the ruled_out of the step that ties the incident to the change that set it off, citing what ruled it out, and never as a step. An earlier change is ruled out only by the service measured healthy with it in place - in metrics read between it and the onset, in an alert that dates the first harm itself at or after a later change (at, where the two instants are the same), or after a confirmed action that left it there - never by how long before the onset it came. Where the record shows none of these, it was not ruled out: say so in that step itself. Stop where the evidence stops.

cites.description: The labels of the evidence that shows this step: T3, G3fa2. Not rows that merely happened at the same time.

ruled_out.description: What else the record ruled out at this step, each what it was and why. Empty on every step but the one that ties the incident to the change that set it off.

cites.description: The labels of what ruled it out.

cause_in_plain_words.description: What caused the incident, in one sentence for a reader who does not work on the service: no component names unless they are unavoidable. When it began, for how long, how bad it got, what customers lost and what was done the document says itself - say none of them. Say only what the record says - of a change, of the service, of the people - and nothing it does not. Where part of it rests only on a reading nothing ran, say that part as likely, in plain words, without mentioning the reading.

cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading.description: Whether the mechanism in root_cause rests on an F row - a reading of the code nothing ran - with no S or D row showing what it rests on. Where you answer true, the document says itself, beside the root cause, that the cause is unverified, and leaves its root-cause review box for a person: say neither in root_cause.

contributing_factors.description: Conditions that had to hold for the incident to happen and did not cause it alone - a safeguard that did not stop it, a gap in detection or review. A factor held before the incident began: what the response did, declined or left behind - an action taken or not, automatic sync left off - is not one; where it went wrong, say it under went_wrong. Not the root cause again in other words: a factor is something that, had it been otherwise, would have stopped or shortened the incident even with what root_cause says still true. A safeguard the record does not show is one not seen, never one absent: write that no check was seen, not that none ran. An alert finds what its rule watches, not the cause behind it: say a fault was found only by what the record shows found it. Each is answered by at least one action item: one of the record's, named in its addressed_by, or one you propose, whose answers name it.

addressed_by.description: The record's own action items that answer it, by the numbers the record gives them: AI-1. Empty where none of them does. Never an item you propose: that item names, in its own answers, the factors it answers.

had_it_been_otherwise.description: What would have gone differently had this been otherwise - stopped, shortened or caught sooner - with what root_cause says still true. A factor that only says the root cause again cannot answer this: leave it out of the list.

label.description: CF-1 for the first factor, CF-2 for the next, and so on in the order you give them. Written here and in an item's answers, never in your prose: the reader never sees it.

lessons.description: What went well, what went wrong, and where the incident got lucky - a risk that went unnoticed this time. Any list may be empty. A safeguard the record does not show is one not seen, never one absent: write that no check was seen, not that none ran. How soon the alert came is weighed by the document already, from what was measured: say nothing of it here.

got_lucky.description: Something the record shows went the fortunate way by chance, and would have made it worse had it not. Empty where the record shows none. Not what kind of fault it was, which the impact already says, nor a limit of what the record shows, which is said in assumptions as what was assumed.

went_well.description: Where one says how quickly Argus did something, write the span as a working of two instants - a T or P row's instant is its first figure, as T3.1 is T3's: {T3.1 - alert_raised}, not in words ("within seconds"). Set the span beside what it times - the thing its later instant dates - not after something else in the same sentence. Name what Code-Fix proposed without saying what it does: the action items and Code-Fix's own reading say that, with its conditions.

went_wrong.description: A change the response left in place on purpose, which one of the record's own action items undoes (automatic sync left off), went as designed and did not go wrong; so did what the design leaves to a person - a draft fix to review and merge. Not a limit of what the record shows - logs nobody read, metrics that stop short of the onset: the document says what was read, and anything assumed is said in assumptions. Not the root cause or a contributing factor again - the document says those already.

reaches_a_cause.description: Whether the chain says why the change that set the incident off broke the service, rather than stopping at that change. A step resting on F rows - a reading of the code nothing ran - counts: whether that leaves the cause unverified is cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading's to say. That a new version does worse is what the change did, not why it broke the service: answer false where the chain says the evidence does not show why.

root_cause.description: What caused the incident, in one or two sentences, written for an engineer who was not on the call: the mechanism - why the change that set it off broke the service, as far as the evidence goes, a missing protection or not. Not the trigger, how it was confirmed, what resolved it or what was ruled out - the document states each of those itself. Not one of the contributing_factors: a safeguard that would have stopped it with this mechanism unchanged is said there, not here. What the service did over the stretch the metrics did not watch is not the mechanism: the document says it itself. Whether it was verified the document says itself, from your answer to cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading - do not say it.

still_at_risk.description: What was still at risk when Argus stopped working on the incident, in one sentence for the same reader - what the fault still in place then could yet do, or the same thing able to happen again. Empty where nothing was. Not whether the service or its metrics were back, nor why - the summary says both. Not what Argus left to a person - a draft fix, automatic sync left off, a recommended action - which the document says itself. Say only what the record says: nothing after Argus stopped was read.

symptom.description: What went wrong as somebody using the service saw it, as short as it can be: it is the document's title. One sentence with no number in it, never over 16 words - the thing that went wrong and what happened to it, with an active verb: 'Account pages failed'. Not the metric the alert fired on, not the cause - the document adds the change it began with itself - and not how it was found, which the document's Detection says. Where nobody using the service saw anything wrong, say that and what was seen instead, in that one sentence.

tools.name: submit_postmortem
